claims.text: A machine-learning framework integrating descriptors of compositional disorder, bonding environments, and local vibrational modes can accurately predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed framework will outperform conventional empirical and ab initio prediction methods.
A hybrid dataset of high-fidelity ab initio phonon-scattering simulations and experimental thermal-conductivity measurements is suitable for training the proposed model.
Phonon conduction dominates under the intended thermal-insulation operating conditions.
The model will be reliable for composition and temperature regimes well represented in its training data.
Intrinsic microstructural disorder and locally varying bonding environments in high-entropy alloys enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering reduces effective thermal conductivity.
The model can learn nonlinear correlations among multi-element disorder descriptors, bonding variations, local vibrational modes, and phonon scattering.
Learning these nonlinear correlations enables the model to predict the effects of composition on phonon scattering more effectively than conventional approaches.
The proposed model will have a narrower prediction-error margin against experimental thermal-conductivity measurements than state-of-the-art methods.
Current empirical correlations and standard ab initio methods inadequately capture scattering mechanisms caused by multi-element disorder in high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced predictive performance is limited to compositions and operating temperatures similar to those in the training dataset.
Predictions for compositions or conditions substantially outside the training domain are uncertain.
Laser-flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance can provide the phonon thermal-conductivity measurements required for the benchmark.
Prediction performance can be compared using mean absolute error or root-mean-square error against experimental measurements.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant prediction-error reduction of approximately 15% or more relative to conventional models across the tested alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
Unpredictable deviations within the validated compositional domain would falsify the hypothesis.
